paragraphs.body: Exposition: Before visiting St. Paul’s Cathedral in Pittsburgh, I imagined it as a tall and ancient building, with golden lights shining through colorful glass windows. I thought it would be a quiet and serious place, like the cathedrals I saw in movies. The name “St. Paul’s Cathedral” made me think of Europe and its old churches, full of history and solemn beauty. I expected to feel a sense of awe and silence as I walked through its grand doors.

paragraphs.body: Conflict: When I finally visited St. Paul’s Cathedral, it was not as I had imagined. The building was beautiful, but the atmosphere felt different. Inside, the people were friendly, and the service was lively. It wasn’t as quiet and serious as I expected. I realized that my idea of a cathedral came from movies and books, not from real life. It surprised me how warm and inviting the place felt. paragraphs.body: Rising Action:This made me think of Tengwang Pavilion (滕王阁) in Nanchang, my hometown. Tengwang Pavilion is also famous and grand, but it is full of life. You can hear the sounds of families, see people taking pictures, and even buy snacks from street vendors nearby. It stands tall with its traditional curved roof and red pillars. Compared to the cathedral, the Pavilion is more open and lively, showing Nanchang’s everyday culture instead of being just a historical monument. Both places are important landmarks, but the atmosphere around them is very different.

Climax:Thinking about both places, I saw how my ideas of Pittsburgh and Nanchang were influenced by stereotypes. I thought all cathedrals were serious and quiet, and I thought all historical places in China were the same. But this comparison showed me how different cultures celebrate history in their own ways. Both places taught me that a place’s real beauty comes from the people and the life around it. I learned that I should experience places with an open mind instead of relying on assumptions.
